newsitem.title: UK: Former UK PM Heath says Conservatives could split.
newsitem.headline: Former UK PM Heath says Conservatives could split.

text.p: Former Conservative premier Edward Heath attacked Prime Minister John Major on Thursday for his lack of leadership on Europe and warned the ruling party risked splitting apart after the looming election.
"The only way we can have a role is through the European Union. We've got to take part. Otherwise there is no world role for Britain," Heath told journalists.
"It is quite frightening because the prime minister is not giving leadership on this. It's because he wants to keep the peace in his party. Well, the leadership isn't there and the peace is lacking."
Heath, who secured Britain's entry into the European Community in 1973, also attacked Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind for saying he was hostile to a European single currency.
"We don't want to break the (Conservative) party... (But) if we have more examples like the foreign secretary, we'll just have to break it.

"It could break after the election," said Heath. Asked if this would still happen if the Conservatives were to win the election, which Major must call by May, he added: "The strains will still be there."
Heath's remarks, at a lunch for foreign correspondents based in London, is likely to increase pressure on Major after Wednesday's cabinet row over the single currency.
The row erupted after Rifkind, apparently breaking a neutral policy agreed by the cabinet in January, said on Wednesday that Britain was "on balance hostile" to EMU (economic and monetary union).
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said his colleague had made "a slip of the tongue", but Rifkind, fanning the dispute, retorted that he had meant what he said.
Both tried to damp down the row, issuing a joint statement to Reuters late on Wednesday night that the government's position had not changed.

But the statement was not enough to calm the anger of pro-European Conservatives like former Foreign Secretary Lord Howe, who attacked Major's apparent hostility towards Europe and hinted he could consider withdrawing support for the government.

Heath lamented the fact that pro-Europeans appeared to have abandoned the public debate, leaving the field open to Eurosceptics in the ruling party who have forced Major into a more antagonistic tone towards Brussels.

"When the foreign secretary said last night the vast majority (of Britons) are against the single currency, he is wrong. The problem in this country is that no-one has explained what a single currency could do," Heath said.

Heath also attacked Rifkind for touring European capitals to spread his Euro-sceptical message. Rifkind was in Bonn for a speech setting out Britain's approach to Europe when he made his remarks about Britain's hostility to a single currency.

"The foreign secretary should not discuss financial questions. That's a matter for the Chancellor of the Exchequer... What's more, he shouldn't be going round Europe and saying he'll talk over the heads of politicians to the people...
"If somebody did that in this country, we'd go mad," Heath said. "It's incredible the foreign secretary is doing this and the sooner he stops the better."
